analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing workers and consumers to arbitrate disputes instead of going to court.
analysis.headline: No action has been taken on the bill since it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on September 15, 2025, with 70 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR Act would make it unenforceable for a company to require, in a job application, employment contract, or product terms of service, that a worker or customer give up their right to go to court over employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights claims. It would also invalidate clauses that bar people from joining class or group lawsuits. Companies could still offer arbitration if a person chooses it after a dispute actually arises, and union-negotiated grievance arbitration stays in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and consumers who today sign away their court rights as a condition of a job or a product. Forcing claims into private arbitration typically means no public court record, no class action to pool small claims, and a decision by an arbitrator chosen under the company's contract. The bill restores access to federal and state courts, including class and collective actions, for discrimination, wage, consumer, and antitrust claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers with forced-arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes predispute arbitration agreements and predispute class-action waivers void and unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, so people can take these claims to court even after signing a contract containing such a clause.

It covers independent contractors as well as employees, and disputes under federal and state civil rights laws, wage laws, and consumer law, including claims seeking class certification under Rule 23 or collective actions under the Fair Labor Standards Act.
It keeps arbitration available when both sides agree to it after a dispute has already arisen, and it preserves arbitration provisions in union collective bargaining agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that currently embed forced-arbitration and class-waiver clauses in employment contracts, terms of service, and consumer agreements. They would face courtroom litigation — including class actions — for claims they now divert into private arbitration, along with the legal exposure and public records that come with it. Arbitration providers would lose a large volume of mandatory-case business.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for an individual claim, and some workers and consumers may prefer it; this bill removes that option in advance, though arbitration remains available by mutual agreement after a dispute arises.

Moving millions of disputes from private arbitration into courtrooms would raise litigation costs for businesses, including small businesses that get sued by customers, and add caseload to already crowded courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade-off is real: some individual disputes may resolve more slowly and at higher cost in court. Against that, forced arbitration plus class-action waivers has meant that many small-dollar harms — illegal fees, wage violations, discrimination — are effectively unremediable because no single worker or customer can afford to pursue a claim alone. Restoring class actions and public court records addresses harms the current system largely absorbs. The carve-outs for voluntary post-dispute arbitration and union contracts limit the bill's disruption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it so far; the current session of Congress runs until January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the Forced Arbitration Injustice Repeal Act of 2025 in the House on September 15, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only action on the bill so far in the record.
Seventy House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed as cosponsors.

Earlier versions of the FAIR Act in previous Congresses similarly gathered Democratic support and did not become law; the 117th Congress version passed the House in 2022 but never received a Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, companies that enforce forced-arbitration and class-waiver clauses keep the status quo: their arbitration requirements remain enforceable and no courtroom remedy has been restored for the workers and consumers subject to them. The bill is pending, not dead, but with no committee action scheduled its prospects in this Congress are poor.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson (D-GA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Act of 2025 and led its introduction in the House.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without committee action since referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 70 cosponsors are House Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican cosponsors appear in the record, and with Republicans holding a 223-217 House majority the bill has no path without Republican support.

industries.industry: Employers using mandatory arbitration (including gig platforms, nursing homes, and large retail and service employers)
industries.note: The bill voids the clauses these companies use to keep employment and consumer claims out of court and away from class actions, restoring workers' and customers' ability to sue publicly. Their interest in keeping the clauses runs against the people subject to them.
Firms that administer mandatory workplace and consumer arbitrations would lose a large, guaranteed stream of cases, since the bill only permits arbitration chosen voluntarily after a dispute arises.

industries.industry: Consumer and plaintiff-side class action law
industries.note: Restoring access to court and to class actions reopens a channel for lawyers to represent workers and consumers whose claims were previously barred, aligning with the bill's benefit to ordinary people.

analysis.trajectory: Previous FAIR Acts in earlier Congresses never became law, and the 117th Congress version passed the House in March 2022 but died without a Senate vote. In the current Congress, Republicans hold a narrow House majority, the bill has no Republican cosponsors, and the Judiciary Committee has taken no action since the September 2025 referral. The most likely outcome is that the bill sits in committee and expires with this Congress unless Democrats retake the chamber or leadership chooses to bring it up.
